title: A-H-V

segments.voice: Yesterday, P-L-L: tefillah, and the verb that turns back on itself. Your line was prayer looks inward. Did you take an honest look at your own part? Day one thousand three hundred sixty-nine.

Seven years is a long time to work for anyone. Jacob agrees to it, working for his uncle Laban, so that he can marry Laban's daughter Rachel. Seven years of flocks, heat, cold nights. And the Torah sums it all up in one sentence: "And Jacob served seven years for Rachel; and they seemed unto him but a few days, for the love he had to her." Years that felt like days. That's what love did to the clock. The word for love in that verse is today's root.
screen: `SEVEN YEARS FOR RACHEL.` → `THEY SEEMED BUT A FEW DAYS.` → `FOR THE LOVE HE HAD TO HER.`

segments.voice: A-H-V. Alef, hey, vet. Ahavah, love. Four verses, four loves. First, love as a feeling strong enough to bend time. That's Jacob. The Torah doesn't hide that this kind of love is real, and that it can change how a whole life feels. Second, love as a command. "And thou shalt love the LORD thy God with all thine heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy might." Those words follow straight after the Shema. And they raise a question teachers have asked: how can anyone be commanded to feel something? One answer the tradition gives is that in the Torah, love is also something you do: with all your heart, your soul and your might, which is to say with your whole life. Third, the neighbor. "Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself: I am the LORD." Tradition says Rabbi Akiva called this verse a great principle of the Torah. Fourth, and later in the same chapter, the stranger. "Thou shalt love him as thyself; for ye were strangers in the land of Egypt." The same words, as thyself, now aimed at the outsider, and given a reason: you know what it's like. So one root holds a young man's longing, a whole people's devotion, the person next door, and the immigrant down the road. Ahavah isn't kept for the ones who are easy to love. And in every one of these verses it's a word you can say, and also a thing you can do.
screen: `LOVE THAT BENDS TIME.` · `WITH ALL THINE HEART.` · `THE NEIGHBOR, AS THYSELF.` · `THE STRANGER, AS THYSELF.` · then, large: `AHAVAH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say "I love you" to someone. First, settle, and breathe. Bring one person to mind, someone you love and don't often say it to. A parent, a friend, a sibling, a child who's grown. See their face. On each breath out, say silently, I love you. Then let the words become a plan: when will you say them out loud, today? A call, a message, a moment at the door. If you pray, you can hold that person in your prayer, by name. The bell holds the time.
A-H-V. Alef, hey, vet: ahavah, love. For Rachel, for God, for the neighbor, and for the stranger. Today's word.
Your line: ahavah. Today, say "I love you" out loud to the person you thought of, and then do one small thing that means it. Day one thousand three hundred sixty-nine.

howItsDone: The paragraph beginning 'and thou shalt love the LORD thy God' is said right after the first line of the Shema, morning and evening, and the blessing just before the Shema speaks of God's love for Israel.
